html:
In 1864 the US Army forced about 8,000 to 9,000 Navajo people to walk some 500 kilometres from their homeland in Arizona and New Mexico to a camp at Bosque Redondo in eastern New Mexico. Hundreds died on the way.

Troops under Kit Carson had burned crops, orchards and flocks to starve the Navajo into surrender. At Bosque Redondo the land was poor, the water bad, and they were held with their enemies the Mescalero Apache. Many died of hunger and disease.

In the Treaty of 1868 the Navajo won the right to return to part of their homeland, which became the largest reservation in the United States. The Long Walk is remembered as a founding trauma, like the Cherokee Trail of Tears.
